claim.name: Claim
claim.definition: The point the writer sets out to prove, stated so someone could disagree with it. Example: “Homework should be banned.”

reason.name: Reason
reason.definition: Why the claim is true: one cause the writer gives for believing it. Example: “First, it takes up the whole evening.”

evidence.name: Evidence
evidence.definition: A fact, number, example or quotation that shows a reason is true. Example: “Students who start at 8:30 sleep an hour more.”

objection.name: Objection
objection.definition: The other side’s case, stated fairly so the writer can answer it. Example: “Some people say homework teaches responsibility.”
objection.opens: begins with the other side’s case

answer.name: Answer
answer.definition: The writer’s reply to an objection. Example: “But responsibility is learned in other ways too.”

call.name: Call
call.definition: What the writer asks the reader to do or believe at the end. Example: “Vote for our side.”
call.opens: begins with what the reader should do
call.then: ends by saying what to do

stakes.name: Stakes
stakes.definition: What is won or lost if the reader agrees or not. Example: “If nothing changes, tired students will keep driving to school.”
stakes.opens: begins with what is at stake

scene.name: Scene
scene.definition: The place, time and people of a story, set down before anything happens. Example: “The party was at Jessica’s house.”

turn.name: Turn
turn.definition: The moment a story changes direction. Example: “Then I heard it again.”
turn.opens: begins at the moment things change

feeling.name: Feeling
feeling.definition: What a person in the story feels, told or shown. Example: “My heart was beating really fast.”

verdict.name: Verdict
verdict.definition: The writer’s judgement of what the story meant, usually at the end. Example: “Maybe I was wrong about him.”

greeting.name: Greeting
greeting.definition: The line that names the person a letter or speech is for. Example: “Dear Mom and Dad,”

news.name: News
news.definition: What the letter tells the reader: what has happened or how things stand. Example: “Camp is okay, I guess.”

request.name: Request
request.definition: What the letter asks the reader to do. Example: “Can you send more snacks?”
request.opens: begins with what it asks for

close.name: Close
close.definition: The sign-off that ends a letter or speech: thanks, a farewell, a name. Example: “Love, Jake”

part.name: Part
part.definition: A paragraph whose job the engine cannot name with confidence.
part.opens: begins without a clear first step
